newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's options for resolving airline dispute.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's options for resolving airline dispute.

text.p: Following is a guide to the negotiations between American Airlines and its pilots who have threatened to strike after midnight Friday if no agreement is reached.
The two sides are negotiating with the help of a mediator who tries to bring the parties to a settlement but does not prescribe one as an arbitrator would.
Arbitration could occur if both the airline and the union agreed to it or if President Clinton imposed it. It would be binding if both parties agreed to abide by the decision.
In 1993, Clinton successfully pressured American Airlines Chairman Robert Crandall into accepting binding arbitration after the airline's flight attendants walked off the job.
In the current dispute, the airline would agree to binding arbitration but the pilots' union opposes it.

Clinton could impose arbitration by establishing a Presidential Emergency Board, which would have 30 days to forge a settlement plan. The airline and the pilots would have another 30 days to consider the plan but during the 60 days there could be no strike or lockout of the pilots by the airline.
If the parties had agreed to accept the result, they would be bound by the arbitrator's ruling. If not, the pilots would be free to strike or the airline could lock them out after the 60 days.

Clinton could decide to establish an emergency board on his own or after a recommendation from the National Mediation Board. Both Clinton and the mediation board have received a confidential report on the national impact of an American Airlines strike from the Department of Transportation.
